title: CI job scheduler with runner heartbeats
name: Build runner scheduler

questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code acquires the job and runner mutexes across its operations? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
A job is cancelled after Next() pops it from the queue but before Assign() is called for it. What happens when Assign runs?
choices: The job is started on the runner anyway, since the queue no longer contains the cancellation.
Assign returns ErrNotPending and the runner stays idle, because the state check happens under both locks.
Assign blocks until the job is re-enqueued.
Assign marks the runner busy and the job is Canceled, leaving the runner stuck.

questions.prompt: reapOne() checks the runner's last heartbeat after taking r.mu, even though ReapStale could have checked it earlier. Why does that matter?
choices: It avoids requeueing a job from a runner that sent a heartbeat between the snapshot and the moment the runner lock was acquired.
It lets ReapStale skip taking the registry lock.
It makes reaping atomic with respect to Enqueue.
It prevents two ReapStale calls from ever running concurrently.

questions.prompt: ReapStale calls s.Enqueue(j) after reapOne returns rather than inside reapOne. What is the effect of that structure?
choices: The job can be lost if the process stops between the two calls.
Enqueue can run concurrently with Assign for the same job without any ordering.
The queue lock is never held while a runner or job lock is held, so qmu cannot take part in a lock cycle with them.
Enqueue is guaranteed to happen before any Heartbeat for that runner.
